calendar_note: Year A. Spring 1 Week 2, 11–15 January 2027. Wednesday 13 January 2027, P3. One 40-minute formative lesson for up to five learners. Spring 1 runs 4 January–12 February for six weeks; Week 6 is assessing. No clock time supplied.

cases.title: A card stand
cases.text: A young person folds a card stand. It falls over after two tries. They say, “I always get this wrong.” An adult says, “The base needs a wider fold.”
cases.barrier: The stand falls over. Repeating the same fold has not solved it.
cases.feedback: The base needs a wider fold.
cases.strategy: Ask the adult to show a wider fold, then test one changed stand.
cases.reason: The change uses the feedback about the base.
cases.growth_line: I have not made it stand yet. I can learn a wider fold.
cases.check: See whether the changed stand stays up. If not, ask for another check.

cases.title: A shape pattern
cases.text: A young person draws a shape pattern. The last part does not match the model after two tries. They say, “I will never do patterns.” Feedback says, “Compare one shape at a time.”
cases.barrier: The last part of the pattern does not match the model.
cases.feedback: Compare one shape at a time.
cases.strategy: Point to the next shape on the model, then draw and check that one shape.
cases.reason: A small comparison can show where the pattern changes.
cases.growth_line: I have not matched it yet. I can check one shape at a time.
cases.check: Compare the new shape with the model. Ask an adult to break down the step if it is still unclear.

cases.title: Explaining a sorting task
cases.text: A young person explains an invented sorting task. The listener cannot follow the order. They say, “I am no good at explaining.” Feedback says, “Give the first step, then pause.”
cases.barrier: The listener cannot follow the order of the explanation.
cases.feedback: Give the first step, then pause.
cases.strategy: Write one clear first step and practise saying it privately to an adult.
cases.reason: One short instruction gives the listener a clear place to start.
cases.growth_line: My explanation is not clear yet. I can practise one step and get feedback.
cases.check: Ask the adult whether the first step is clear. They can help rewrite it or agree another response mode.

worked_examples_status: All worked examples, people and quoted feedback are invented. Generic objects and tasks only. No real person, product, platform or place is represented.
private_help_route: Ask a trusted adult privately or use the school’s help route. Point to HELP, write a request or say “Can we talk in private?” If one adult is busy or help is insufficient, use the route to another trusted adult. No need to keep trying alone before asking. Offer pass, a supported pause and a neutral task with a return plan.
typed_and_scribed_routes: Either choice can use the editable Evidence Sheet page 2, Type instead. Type in the blank prompts or the Support note if chosen cell. Save using the usual routine, lesson code and work reference; show the adult privately. Book or aid remains valid. A scribe records exact words or selections, reads back quietly and allows correction.
worked_example_and_fade: Read A. Name the difficulty and the useful feedback. Model: “Resilience means finding a way forward when things are hard, with support when needed. The stand falls over. They can ask for a wider-fold model, then try that change. It uses the feedback.” Add the realistic learning line. Check privately whether the model changes a step or just repeats it. For guided work, match feedback to the next step or improve “Try harder in the same way”. Reduce answer cues while keeping the model and word bank.
adaptations: Cognition and Learning: read one part, highlight the feedback and keep a visible model. Communication and Interaction: allow processing time, short choices, a communication aid and sentence frames. SEMH: calm predictable stages, pass, supported pause and neutral task. Sensory and Physical: accessible text, usual aids and comfortable response position. EAL: teach word meanings, read together and plan in any language. Colour carries no answer meaning.
misconceptions: “Resilience means never stopping”: a planned pause, support or a changed goal can be useful. “Try harder guarantees success”: useful feedback and access matter; outcomes are uncertain. “Not yet is enough”: add a concrete next step. “Help means failure”: adults can help remove barriers. Stop and seek help if a task is unsafe or overwhelming.

main_hinge.claim: Use feedback and change one step after an unsuccessful attempt.

parallel_hinge.claim: Asking for help can be part of resilience.

success: Explain resilience as finding a way forward through difficulty, with support where needed.
Give one feasible strategy and a reason linked to the case.
Add a realistic learning line with a next action and recognise a private help route.

evidence.description: Dated next step map for B or support note for C: explanation of resilience, difficulty, one feasible strategy with a reason, realistic learning line and private help. Keep actual access, answer cues, first thinking, one next step and reply.

assessment: Judge the explanation of resilience and the chosen strategy separately. Secure explanation includes finding a way forward through difficulty, with support if needed. Secure application gives one feasible strategy linked to the case and explains its purpose. A realistic learning line shows growth-mindset understanding. Record help-route knowledge alongside these. Partial evidence is retained honestly. No response, including a pass, is unobserved. Do not grade personality, obedience, optimism or actual resilience from this fictional task.
where_this_leads: This helps me use feedback, change a plan and ask for support when learning a skill or doing future work.

paragraphs_in_document_order: Wednesday 13 January 2027 · P3 · 40 minutes · Year A
GROW · up to five learners · Spring 1 Week 2 · formative
Theme: Resilience & Change. Spring 1 has six weeks. Week 6 is assessing.
Thread tags: SMSC S/So (M/C: none); British Values IL/MR (D/RL/T: none).
Build personal resilience and a growth mindset.
Source: GROW Weekly - Spring, PSHE, row 65. B65 Spr1·W2; C65 exact outcome. The generic strand heading is PSHE & Citizenship in A64; D64–F64 supply shared context. Names are omitted.
Describe what resilience means and one way to keep going when something is hard.

Both task choices explain resilience, name a difficulty in an invented case, and give one useful next step with a reason. Add a realistic learning line and a private help route. These are lesson evidence, not proof of a lasting personal trait.

Books, pens, Support Cards and Vocabulary Mat for up to five learners. Optional editable Evidence Sheet for typing; no login or internet needed. Arrange private response turns. Confirm an available trusted adult, the school’s help route and a supported pause. The card stand, pattern and sorting task are written fictional examples; no practical equipment or real task performance is required.

Use only invented stories. Do not ask for personal setbacks, trauma, family circumstances, stress scores or public examples. Resilience can include support, changing approach and a planned pause. Never require persistence in something unsafe or overwhelming. Avoid promises that effort or positive words guarantee success.
This helps me use feedback, change a plan and ask for support when learning a skill or doing future work.
Settle, confirm private help; choose an action or explain its fit.
Read exact outcome; explain resilience and growth mindset.
Model A, then match feedback or improve unhelpful advice.
Check flexible persistence and help; choose task and response mode.
Next step map B or support note C, in a book, typed, aided or scribed.
Check work or improve a model; retain one next step and reply.
Explain resilience or correct a myth about help.
Total 40 minutes. Brief pauses and processing time sit inside these phases. Slides 7 and 8 are alternatives in one 12-minute work period. Optional help slide 11 and hidden staff slide 12 add no time.

Retrieve Week 1 with an invented learner who has too many instructions. Choose “ask for one step” or “hide the problem”, or explain why asking for one step may help. Accept a private selection, typing or a scribe. If Week 1 was missed, read the full example without expecting recall.

Read A. Name the difficulty and the useful feedback. Model: “Resilience means finding a way forward when things are hard, with support when needed. The stand falls over. They can ask for a wider-fold model, then try that change. It uses the feedback.” Add the realistic learning line. Check privately whether the model changes a step or just repeats it. For guided work, match feedback to the next step or improve “Try harder in the same way”. Reduce answer cues while keeping the model and word bank.

Offer choice 1 next step map for B and choice 2 support note for C. Both meet the same success checks. Say and show Type instead. Learners may change choice. For review, use the checklist or improve “Just keep going. You will get it right.” Give one precise next step and retain the reply. No public performance is required.

Choose either main task. Read one short part at a time with the word bank, sentence starters and A model. Offer two strategy options if needed. Point, use an aid, type or use an exact scribe. Record answer cues apart from normal access.

Choose either main task. Explain resilience, identify the barrier, give one fitting strategy with a reason, and add a realistic learning line and private help. Keep the model, bank and normal reading/typing aids available.
Choose either main task. Explain how to check whether the step helps, and what support or change may be needed if it does not. No extra personal disclosure or public speaking.

Main A: after an unsuccessful try, ask for feedback and change one step. B: repeat the same action without checking. Key A. Ask why privately. If unclear, return to A’s wider-fold feedback. Parallel A: help means the learner has failed. B: help can be part of resilience. Key B. Silence or a pass is unobserved.

Cognition and Learning: read one part, highlight the feedback and keep a visible model. Communication and Interaction: allow processing time, short choices, a communication aid and sentence frames. SEMH: calm predictable stages, pass, supported pause and neutral task. Sensory and Physical: accessible text, usual aids and comfortable response position. EAL: teach word meanings, read together and plan in any language. Colour carries no answer meaning.

Prompt ladder: 1 point to place/instruction; 2 ask a short question privately; 3 rephrase; 4 offer scaffold/choice; 5 model the first step only, then return the task. Log content help. In input, clarify the terms; in guided work, elicit the feedback link; in individual work, record access separately from an adult-supplied answer.

Ask a trusted adult privately or use the school’s help route. Point to HELP, write a request or say “Can we talk in private?” If one adult is busy or help is insufficient, use the route to another trusted adult. No need to keep trying alone before asking. Offer pass, a supported pause and a neutral task with a return plan.

Either choice can use the editable Evidence Sheet page 2, Type instead. Type in the blank prompts or the Support note if chosen cell. Save using the usual routine, lesson code and work reference; show the adult privately. Book or aid remains valid. A scribe records exact words or selections, reads back quietly and allows correction.

Judge the explanation of resilience and the chosen strategy separately. Secure explanation includes finding a way forward through difficulty, with support if needed. Secure application gives one feasible strategy linked to the case and explains its purpose. A realistic learning line shows growth-mindset understanding. Record help-route knowledge alongside these. Partial evidence is retained honestly. No response, including a pass, is unobserved. Do not grade personality, obedience, optimism or actual resilience from this fictional task.

“Resilience means never stopping”: a planned pause, support or a changed goal can be useful. “Try harder guarantees success”: useful feedback and access matter; outcomes are uncertain. “Not yet is enough”: add a concrete next step. “Help means failure”: adults can help remove barriers. Stop and seek help if a task is unsafe or overwhelming.

Give one NS: explain the word; use the feedback; make the step specific; add a reason. Keep first thinking and reply. VF verbal feedback; WS worked with support; I independent; // self-edit; ? read back; E actual banked evidence. R only after Voice, Audience, NS and response in own colour or usual recorded mode. Offer to the Communication portfolio.

Confirm the available route before teaching. Listen calmly, avoid probing or public discussion, do not promise secrecy and follow the school’s usual procedure. Seek immediate on-site support for urgent concerns. Keep concerns out of shared work. No named services or helplines. This lesson teaches a concept and a strategy, not treatment or a proven change in wellbeing. Any accredited mapping needs actual evidence and staff confirmation. Next is GROW PSHE Week 3, row 66, after Downloaded.

Build personal resilience and a growth mindset.
Describe what resilience means and one way to keep going when something is hard.

Accept resilience as finding a way forward, adapting or recovering when things are hard, with support where needed. A growth mindset allows for skills to develop through useful practice, feedback and support. Avoid fixed labels for learners or claims that positive words, effort alone or this lesson guarantee improvement.

Starter: ask for one step. It reduces the amount to follow. A’s difficulty is a stand that falls over; feedback identifies the narrow base. A feasible next step is to ask for a wider-fold model and test that change. “I have not made it stand yet. I can learn a wider fold” adds a concrete action. A planned pause and adult support are valid if needed.

Match a wider fold to changing the base. To improve “try harder in the same way”, use a wider-fold model, change the base and check the result. Check after modelling: the useful step changes the approach using feedback. Repeating without checking does not use the available information. Accept equivalent words.

Main A: use feedback and change one step. Parallel B: asking for help can be part of resilience. If unclear, point back to A’s specific feedback, re-model one step and repeat privately. Keep normal access aids. A pass is unobserved.

No personal setbacks, trauma stories, stress scores, public voting or compulsory real-world performance. Do not equate persistence with obedience or staying in an unsafe situation. A pause, a different approach, an adjusted task or more support may be needed. No clinical or treatment claims.
Two choices with the same learning

Explain resilience in plain words. Barrier: the pattern does not match. Strategy: compare the model one shape at a time, then draw/check that shape. Reason: a small comparison helps locate the mismatch. Learning line: “I have not matched it yet. I can check one shape at a time.” Private help: ask a trusted adult to make the step clearer. A different feasible strategy is acceptable if the reason fits.

“Resilience means finding a way forward when things are hard, with support if needed. The listener cannot follow the order. You could write and practise one clear first step with an adult. This gives the listener a place to start. Your explanation is not clear yet, but you can practise one step and get feedback. Ask a trusted adult in private for help.” Accept a typed or aided explanation agreed with the adult.

Both choices explain resilience, link one feasible strategy to a barrier, and add a realistic learning line and private help. A map needs no polished diagram; a note needs no extra length. Usual reading, typing and scribing do not remove independence of thought. Log adult-supplied content separately.

Improve “Just keep going. You will get it right” by naming a specific change and reason, without guaranteeing success. Example: compare one shape with the model to find the mismatch. Exit: resilience can involve a new approach and help; asking for help does not mean failure.

B: compare the next shape; if still unclear, ask for a model or smaller step. C: ask whether the first instruction is clear; if not, get feedback or agree another response mode. Check the strategy, not the person’s worth. A useful next step may need changing.

Record explanation and strategy application separately. Secure explanation includes adapting or finding a way forward through difficulty, with support if needed. Secure strategy evidence gives one feasible next step and why it fits the case. Record the realistic learning line and help route alongside these. Do not claim the learner has become resilient or changed a lasting mindset from one response. Partial evidence is retained. No response, including a pass, is unobserved.

Editable Evidence Sheet page 2 has blank fields for the map and a Support note if chosen cell. Offer typing for either task. Save with the usual routine, lesson code and work reference. If typing is unavailable, use a book, aid or exact scribe. Read the response back privately and allow correction.

Give one NS such as adding a reason or making the step specific. Retain first thinking and reply. R follows Voice, Audience, NS and response; E means actual work saved. Offer to the Communication portfolio. Staff confirm any accredited mapping.

Use a trusted adult and the school’s help route. Point to HELP, type or write a private request, or use an aid. If one adult is busy or help is insufficient, use the route to another. No need to keep trying alone. Listen calmly, avoid probing or secrecy promises, and follow usual procedures. Keep concerns outside shared evidence. Stop and get immediate on-site support for urgent concerns.
